title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms - Unit II: Divide & Conquer, Greedy Method

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: Binary search operates on sorted arrays by recursively or iteratively halving the search interval using the midpoint formula mid = low + (high - low) / 2, resulting in a time complexity of O(log n) defined by the recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: This target assesses the student's conceptual understanding of how the divide-and-conquer strategy reduces problem size and why the specific midpoint calculation is necessary to prevent integer overflow while maintaining logarithmic efficiency.
misconception_distractor_hints: Assuming binary search works on unsorted arrays by simply comparing the middle element.
Calculating the midpoint as (low + high) / 2 without recognizing the risk of integer overflow for large indices.
Believing the time complexity is O(n) because the algorithm traverses the array, ignoring the halving of the search space.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: The median of two sorted arrays is determined by finding a partition point where the left half contains the smaller elements and the right half contains the larger elements, calculating the median as (max(left_half) + min(right_half)) / 2.0 for even lengths or max(left_half) for odd lengths.
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: This target evaluates the student's ability to apply binary search logic to a complex partitioning problem, demonstrating how to efficiently locate the median without merging the arrays, which would result in O(n) complexity.
misconception_distractor_hints: Merging the two arrays into a single sorted array and then finding the median, which is inefficient and defeats the purpose of the divide-and-conquer approach.
Incorrectly identifying the partition boundaries, leading to a median calculation that includes elements from the wrong half.
Assuming the median is always the average of the two middle elements of the individual arrays, ignoring the combined sorted order.

assessment_targets.what_taught_summary: The fixed point problem involves finding an index i in a sorted array where A[i] = i by applying binary search logic: if arr[mid] < mid, search the right half; if arr[mid] > mid, search the left half; if equal, return mid.
assessment_targets.why_assessed_pedagogy: This target assesses the student's ability to adapt standard binary search conditions to a specific property (index-value equality), demonstrating the flexibility of the divide-and-conquer paradigm in solving non-trivial search problems.
misconception_distractor_hints: Searching for the value equal to the index in an unsorted manner or using linear search, ignoring the sorted property that enables binary search.
Incorrectly adjusting the search bounds, such as searching the left half when arr[mid] < mid, which contradicts the monotonic nature of the difference A[i] - i.
Assuming a fixed point always exists in any sorted array, failing to handle the case where no such index is found.
